title: Common Child
directAnswer: A 'common child' of two strings is a string that is a subsequence of both — so the answer is the length of the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS). Build a 2D table dp where dp[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i characters of s1 and the first j of s2. When the current characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). The answer is dp[m][n]. O(m·n) time, O(m·n) space (reducible to O(min(m,n))).

remember.pattern: Longest Common Subsequence — classic 2D table DP
rules: A 'child' is a **subsequence** (delete characters, keep order) — NOT a substring. Characters need not be contiguous.
On a character **match**, you extend the diagonal: `dp[i-1][j-1] + 1`. The +1 is the matched character.
On a **mismatch**, you drop one character from one string: `max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`. Never add 1 on a mismatch.
Use **1-based** indexing for the table with an extra row/column of zeros — it removes all the `i==0` / `j==0` boundary checks.
You only need the length here, not the string itself, so the standard table suffices (no backtracking required).
whenToUse: Two sequences, asked for the longest order-preserving common part
Edit-distance / diff style problems (insert, delete, match)
You can frame progress as 'consume one character from one or both strings'
antiSignals: It must be **contiguous** → that's Longest Common Substring (reset to 0 on mismatch, track a global max)
Only one string is involved → likely LIS or palind, not LCS
Sequences are huge (10⁶+) and you need exact LCS → O(m·n) may be too slow; bit-parallel / Hunt–Szymanski needed
You need the actual matched string, not its length → keep the table and backtrack from dp[m][n]
remember.takeaway: LCS is the canonical two-sequence grid DP. Match → take the diagonal plus one; mismatch → take the better of dropping a character from either string. Once you internalise this 2×2 cell rule you can solve Edit Distance, Shortest Common Supersequence, and diff tools with the same table.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise 'common child' as a thin disguise for Longest Common Subsequence, set up the 2D recurrence correctly, and know subsequence (gaps allowed) differs from substring (contiguous).
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Solving Longest Common Substring instead (resetting to 0 on mismatch), or adding 1 on a mismatch, or confusing the diagonal/up/left transitions.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the recurrence from the recursion tree, note the overlapping subproblems that justify DP, then mention the O(min(m,n)) two-row space optimisation and how backtracking would recover the actual child string.

problemStatement:
A string is said to be a **child** of another string if it can be formed by **deleting zero or more characters** from the parent (the remaining characters keep their original order). In other words, a child is a subsequence.

Given two strings `s1` and `s2` of equal length consisting of uppercase English letters, find the **length of the longest string** that is a child of *both* `s1` and `s2`.
constraints: Both strings contain only uppercase English letters A–Z
Return the length of the longest common child (a subsequence, not a substring)
understanding: We want the longest sequence of letters that appears in both strings in the same relative order, allowing gaps. This is exactly the Longest Common Subsequence. The key reframing: at each step compare the last unprocessed character of each prefix — if they match, that letter can end a common child and we recurse on both shorter prefixes; if they differ, at least one of those two characters cannot be part of an optimal child ending here, so we try dropping each and keep the better result.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is a 'child' a contiguous substring or a subsequence?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A subsequence — we delete characters and keep order, gaps allowed. This is the single most important clarification; mistaking it for a substring gives a completely different (smaller) answer.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need to return the actual common child string or just its length?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the length for this problem. The actual string can be recovered by backtracking through the table if asked.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the two strings guaranteed to be the same length?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: On HackerRank, yes. The algorithm works for unequal lengths too — the table is just (m+1)×(n+1).

clarifyingQuestions.question: What characters can appear?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Only uppercase A–Z. That doesn't change the algorithm but bounds the alphabet if you wanted to optimise.

examples.explanation: The longest common child is "AY" (also "RY"... actually "AY": A appears in HARRY at index 1 and in SALLY at index 1; Y is last in both). Length 2.
No common letters at all, so the only common child is the empty string of length 0.

diagrams.caption: Every cell of the LCS table follows one of two rules depending on whether the current characters are equal.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Plain Recursion (Exponential)
approaches.whenToMention: State it first to derive the recurrence, then point out the exponential blow-up from recomputed subproblems to motivate DP.
hints: Compare the last character of each prefix. If they're equal, that character can extend the common child — recurse on both prefixes minus their last char and add 1.
If the last characters differ, at least one of them isn't used as the final matched character. Try dropping the last char of s1, then dropping the last char of s2, and keep the larger result.
Base case: if either prefix is empty, the LCS is 0. This recursion is correct but recomputes the same (i, j) pair exponentially many times.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each mismatch branches into two recursive calls, so the recursion tree has up to 2^(m+n) leaves. The same (i, j) subproblem is solved over and over — that redundancy is exactly what DP removes.
approaches.explanation:
Define `lcs(i, j)` = length of the longest common child of the first `i` characters of `s1` and the first `j` characters of `s2`.

**Match case.** If `s1[i-1] == s2[j-1]`, the two prefixes end in the same letter. That letter can always be the last character of an optimal common child of these prefixes, so `lcs(i, j) = lcs(i-1, j-1) + 1`. We never need to consider *not* using a matched ending character — using it is never worse.

**Mismatch case.** If the last characters differ, they cannot both be the final matched letter (they're different letters), so at least one of them is not the ending of the optimal child. We don't know which, so we try both: `lcs(i-1, j)` (the optimal child doesn't end with `s1`'s last char) and `lcs(i, j-1)` (it doesn't end with `s2`'s last char), and take the maximum.

**Base case.** An empty prefix shares nothing, so `lcs(0, j) = lcs(i, 0) = 0`.

**Why it's too slow.** On a full mismatch chain every call spawns two children, producing an exponential tree. But notice there are only `(m+1)(n+1)` distinct `(i, j)` pairs — the tree revisits them enormously. That overlap is the signal to memoise, which turns the recursion into the table below.
approaches.insight: The recurrence has only two shapes — diagonal+1 on a match, max of up/left on a mismatch. Recognising that there are merely (m+1)(n+1) distinct states is what tells you this exponential recursion collapses into a polynomial DP.

pitfalls: Adding 1 on a mismatch — only a match contributes a character.
Recursing without memoisation at |s| = 5000 — exponential, times out instantly.
Treating it as a substring problem (resetting on mismatch) — solves the wrong question.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up 2D Table (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'fill an (m+1)×(n+1) table where each cell is match→diagonal+1, else max of up/left'.
hints: Memoise the recursion: there are only (m+1)(n+1) distinct (i, j) states, so build a table dp[i][j] instead of recomputing.
Add a row and column of zeros (the empty-prefix base case) so you never index out of bounds and never special-case i==0 or j==0.
Fill row by row: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 on a match, else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). The answer is dp[m][n].
approaches.complexityReasoning: Exactly (m+1)(n+1) cells, each computed in O(1) from three already-known neighbours → O(m·n) time. The full table is O(m·n) space; keeping only the previous and current rows reduces it to O(min(m,n)).
approaches.explanation:
Turn the recurrence into a table. Let `dp[i][j]` be the LCS length of `s1[0..i)` and `s2[0..j)`. Row `0` and column `0` are all zeros — those encode the empty-prefix base case.

**Filling a cell.** For `i, j ≥ 1`, look at the two current characters `s1[i-1]` and `s2[j-1]`:
- If they're **equal**, the best common child of these prefixes is the best child of the shorter prefixes plus this shared letter: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1`.
- If they **differ**, the optimal child can't end with both, so drop one and take the better: `dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`.

Each cell depends only on its diagonal, top, and left neighbours, all filled earlier in a row-major sweep, so a single pass top-to-bottom, left-to-right is enough.

**Why the table is correct and minimal.** The recursion above is provably correct; memoising it can't change the answer, only the running time. Because every cell is computed exactly once from O(1) neighbours, the whole table is O(m·n) — comfortably fast for the 5000×5000 worst case (~25M cells).

**Space optimisation.** Cell `dp[i][j]` only ever reads row `i` and row `i-1`. So you can keep just two rows (or even one row plus a saved diagonal), dropping memory from O(m·n) to O(min(m,n)). State that as the follow-up — it's the difference between 100 MB and a few KB at the size limit.
approaches.insight: Each cell reads only its diagonal, top, and left neighbour. That locality is what makes the row-major fill valid in one pass and what enables the two-row O(min(m,n)) space trick: you never look further back than the previous row.

pitfalls: Resetting dp[i][j] to 0 on a mismatch — that solves Longest Common *Substring*, not subsequence.
Allocating a 5001×5001 int table in a language with tight memory — use the two-row optimisation if needed.
Off-by-one: dp indices are 1-based but string indices are 0-based — always read s1[i-1], s2[j-1].

approaches.name: Two-Row Space Optimisation
approaches.whenToMention: Mention as the memory-savvy refinement once the 2D table is on the board — useful at the 5000×5000 limit.
hints: Notice dp[i][j] only reads the current row i and the previous row i-1 — rows older than i-1 are never touched again.
Keep just two 1D arrays, prev and curr, of length n+1. After finishing row i, copy curr into prev (or swap the references).
Iterate the outer loop over the longer string and size the rows by the shorter string to make the arrays as small as possible.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Same (m·n) cell computations, but at any moment only two rows of length n+1 exist → O(min(m,n)) space when you loop over the longer dimension.
approaches.explanation:
The full 2D table wastes memory: every cell only depends on the row above it and the cell to its left in the current row. So we keep two rolling arrays.

**prev** holds row `i-1`; **curr** is the row `i` we're building. For each `j`: a match uses `prev[j-1] + 1` (the diagonal), a mismatch uses `max(prev[j], curr[j-1])` (up and left). After completing a row, swap `curr` into `prev` and reuse the buffer.

**Why it's identical in answer.** We never read any value older than the previous row, so discarding earlier rows is information-lossless. The numbers computed are exactly the same as the full table; only storage changes.

**When it matters.** At |s1| = |s2| = 5000, the full `int[5001][5001]` table is ~100 MB. Two rows are ~40 KB. If a judge or interviewer flags memory, this is the fix — and looping the outer dimension over the longer string keeps the rows as short as possible, giving O(min(m,n)).
approaches.insight: Rolling two rows is the standard space cut for any grid DP whose recurrence reaches back exactly one row. The moment you confirm 'no cell reads further than row i-1', you've earned the right to throw away everything older.

pitfalls: Forgetting to reset/overwrite curr[0] — it must stay 0 (the empty-prefix column).
Reading the wrong buffer after the swap — the answer is in prev[n] (post-swap), not curr[n].
Not reusing the buffer (allocating a new row each iteration) — correct but defeats the memory goal.

commonMistakes: Solving Longest Common Substring (contiguous) instead of subsequence — resetting the cell to 0 on a mismatch.
Adding 1 to the answer on a mismatch instead of only on a match.
Running the bare recursion at |s| = 5000 without memoisation — exponential blow-up.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Substring instead of subsequence
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Resetting dp[i][j] to 0 on a mismatch computes the longest *contiguous* common run. "HARRY"/"SALLY" then returns 1 (just one matching letter run) instead of 2 for the subsequence "AY".
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if (s1.charAt(i-1) == s2.charAt(j-1)) dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1;
else dp[i][j] = 0;  // longest common SUBSTRING, wrong problem
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if (s1.charAt(i-1) == s2.charAt(j-1)) dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1;
else dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Adding 1 on a mismatch
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Only a matched character contributes length. Adding 1 in the max branch overcounts and produces lengths longer than either string.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: No memoisation on the recursion
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The plain recursion revisits each (i, j) exponentially. At |s| = 5000 it never finishes. Either memoise the recursion or write the bottom-up table.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
def lcs(i, j):
    if i == 0 or j == 0: return 0
    if s1[i-1] == s2[j-1]: return lcs(i-1, j-1) + 1
    return max(lcs(i-1, j), lcs(i, j-1))  # recomputes everything

patternNote: Longest Common Subsequence is the prototypical two-sequence grid DP. Match → diagonal + 1; mismatch → max of up and left. Recognise it whenever two sequences are compared for an order-preserving overlap, and remember the contiguous variant (Longest Common Substring) resets to 0 on a mismatch instead.
